tldr:
Hooks are **your code at fixed points in the agent loop**. **PreToolUse** runs **before** a tool call: return `permissionDecision: "deny"` with a **reason that says what to do instead** (e.g. escalate to a human). Return `{}` to let the call through. **PostToolUse** runs **after** the tool: return `updatedToolOutput` so the model sees **one consistent format** (ISO 8601 dates, named statuses). The exam point: **hooks give deterministic guarantees; prompt instructions give probabilistic compliance.** Mechanics from the docs:

- Matchers match **tool names** (`mcp__server__tool`; a plain `process_refund` is an exact name).
- One **deny** beats every allow.
- PostToolUse **can't undo** an action that already ran.
- **async** hooks can't block.
mentalModel: A hook is a checkpoint on the conveyor belt, not a sign on the wall. The prompt is the sign — most people read it, someone in a hurry doesn't. PreToolUse is the gate **before** the machine: it stops the part and points to the right line. PostToolUse is the station **after** it: it can relabel the part, but it can't un-make it.
whatItIs:
The exam guide covers Agent SDK hooks for intercepting tool calls and normalising data (Guide §6 · TS 1.5, p.7). The Agent SDK
and Claude Code docs define the events, the decisions and the matcher rules.

**Sub-concepts — each with its picture to remember**

| # | Sub-concept | 🧭 Mental model | ⭐ Exam reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hook vs prompt instruction | The gate vs the sign on the wall — a sign is usually obeyed; a gate always is. | ⭐ TS 1.5 · Knowledge 3, Skill 3 |
| 2 | PreToolUse (tool call interception) | The gate before the machine: it can stop the part or send it elsewhere. | ⭐ TS 1.5 · Knowledge 2 |
| 3 | deny + reason + redirect | A closed gate with a sign saying which door to use — or people keep pushing it. | ⭐ TS 1.5 · Skill 2 |
| 4 | PostToolUse + updatedToolOutput | The relabelling station after the machine: one label format for everyone downstream. | ⭐ TS 1.5 · Knowledge 1, Skill 1 |
| 5 | PostToolUse can't undo | The part is already made — relabelling won't un-make it. | 📘 docs |
| 6 | Matchers | The gate checks the badge name exactly; `process_refund` isn't `mcp__billing__process_refund`. | 📘 docs |
| 7 | Several hooks: deny wins | One guard saying no closes the gate, however many say yes. | 📘 docs |
| 8 | Async hooks | A guard who waves you through and files a report later — they can't stop anything. | 📘 docs |

**Hooks vs prompt instructions** (the comparison CLAUDE.md requires)

| # | Aspect | Hook (PreToolUse / PostToolUse) | Prompt instruction |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Guarantee | Deterministic — runs on every matching call | Probabilistic — usually followed |
| 2 | Where it runs | Your code, outside the model | Inside the model's reasoning |
| 3 | Pressure from the user | No effect (“my manager approved it”) | Can talk the model out of it |
| 4 | Can block an action | Yes (PreToolUse deny) | No — it can only ask |
| 5 | Can reshape tool data | Yes (PostToolUse updatedToolOutput) | Only by asking the model to convert |
| 6 | Judgment calls | — (rules only) | ✓ tone, wording, nuance |
| 7 | Use it for | ⭐ Business rules that must hold; data normalisation | Guidance, style, preferences |
| 8 | Exam reference | TS 1.5 · Knowledge 3, Skill 3 | TS 1.5 · Knowledge 3 |

**PreToolUse vs PostToolUse** (docs)

| # | Aspect | PreToolUse | PostToolUse |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fires | Before the tool runs | After the tool succeeded |
| 2 | Can block the action | Yes — `permissionDecision: "deny"` | No — the action already happened |
| 3 | Can change | The input (`updatedInput`) | The output (`updatedToolOutput`), or append `additionalContext` |
| 4 | Guide example | Block refunds over $500, redirect to a human | Normalise Unix / ISO 8601 / numeric codes |
| 5 | Decisions | allow · deny · ask · defer (deny wins) | — |
howItWorks:
1. **Register** callbacks per event in `hooks = {"PreToolUse": [HookMatcher(matcher=..., hooks=[fn])], ...}`. A matcher is an
   exact tool name, an `|` list of names, or a regex (`mcp__billing__.*`). Omit it to run for every tool.
2. **The model requests a tool.** Every matching PreToolUse hook runs; if **any** returns `deny`, the call is blocked and the
   `permissionDecisionReason` goes to the model as the result.
3. **Put the alternative in the reason** (“call escalate_to_human instead”) so the model redirects rather than retries.
4. **Return `{}`** when the input is within policy — the call runs unchanged.
5. **The tool runs;** matching PostToolUse hooks get `tool_response` and can return `updatedToolOutput` (replace) or
   `additionalContext` (append) before the model reads it.
6. **Keep the prompt rule too** for explanation and tone — but the hook is what guarantees it.
whereSeen:
- **Scenario 1 — Customer Support Resolution Agent** (Guide §5, p.3): refund limits enforced by hooks, redirected to humans.
- **Scenario 3 — Multi-Agent Research System** (Guide §5, p.4): normalising data from several MCP tools before the agent reasons.
- **Scenario 4 — Developer Productivity with Claude** (Guide §5, p.4): hooks that guard file writes and shell commands.

docsRefs.title: Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks (Agent SDK)
Automate actions with hooks — deterministic control; limitations

grounding.text: Hooks are callbacks registered per event in options.hooks as {event: [HookMatcher(matcher, hooks=[callback])]}; a callback receives (input_data, tool_use_id, context) and returns a dict — {} lets the operation proceed unchanged.
PreToolUse fires on a tool call request and can block or modify it: hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision (allow / deny / ask / defer), permissionDecisionReason and updatedInput.
permissionDecisionReason tells the model why a call was denied, so it avoids retrying; systemMessage is shown to the user, not the model.
grounding.ref: agent-sdk/hooks § Add context and block a tool; systemMessage not appearing

grounding.text: PostToolUse fires after a tool returns: additionalContext appends information to the result; updatedToolOutput replaces the output before Claude sees it, for any tool (updatedMCPToolOutput is the deprecated MCP-only field).
PostToolUse hooks can't undo actions, because the tool has already executed.

When several hooks or permission rules apply, deny beats defer, which beats ask, which beats allow; one deny blocks the call. Matching hooks run in parallel in no guaranteed order, so write each one to stand alone.
grounding.ref: agent-sdk/hooks § Outputs note; Register multiple hooks

grounding.text: Matchers: '*', '' or omitted match everything; a value made only of letters, digits, _, -, spaces, commas and | is compared as an exact tool name (or list of names); anything else is an unanchored regular expression. MCP tools are named mcp__<server>__<tool>; 'mcp__memory' alone matches nothing — use 'mcp__memory__.*'. Matchers see tool names only, not arguments.
grounding.ref: hooks § Matcher patterns; agent-sdk/hooks § Matcher not filtering as expected

grounding.text: An async hook output lets the agent continue immediately; it can't block, modify or add context — use it only for side effects like logging.
Fields such as updatedInput must sit inside hookSpecificOutput, with hookEventName; top-level placement is a listed reason the change isn't applied.

Hooks run before every other permission step (deny rules, ask rules, mode, allow rules, canUseTool); a hook deny applies even in bypassPermissions mode, while a hook allow does not skip deny/ask rules.
Hooks give deterministic control: certain actions always happen rather than relying on the model choosing to do them.

Hook patterns such as PostToolUse intercept tool results to transform them before the model processes them; hooks that intercept outgoing tool calls enforce compliance rules (e.g. blocking refunds above a threshold); hooks give deterministic guarantees while prompt instructions give probabilistic compliance.

Skills: PostToolUse hooks that normalise heterogeneous formats (Unix timestamps, ISO 8601, numeric status codes) from different MCP tools; interception hooks that block policy-violating actions (refunds over $500) and redirect to an alternative workflow (human escalation); choosing hooks over prompts when compliance must be guaranteed.
The guide says 'tool call interception'; the docs' event for it is PreToolUse, with allow/deny/ask/defer decisions.
Putting the redirect instruction (call escalate_to_human) in permissionDecisionReason is this page's way of applying the guide's 'redirect to an alternative workflow'.

The customers, MCP servers and data are invented. So is the model's behaviour: a prompt-only rule slips when the customer claims prior approval; raw Unix timestamps and numeric codes are misread; without a reason a denied call is retried. Real models are probabilistic — the lab makes one bad outcome repeatable.

examPoints.text: Hook patterns like PostToolUse intercept tool results and transform them before the model processes them.
Hook patterns that intercept outgoing tool calls enforce compliance rules (e.g. blocking refunds above a threshold).
Hooks give deterministic guarantees; prompt instructions give only probabilistic compliance.
Write PostToolUse hooks that normalise mixed formats (Unix timestamps, ISO 8601, numeric status codes) from different MCP tools.
Write interception hooks that block policy-violating actions (refunds over $500) and redirect to another workflow (human escalation).
Choose hooks over prompt-based enforcement when business rules need guaranteed compliance.

labIntro:
You write two hooks and register them. The **simulated** support agent then handles three customers: one pushing an **$800
refund “already approved by a manager”**, one with an ordinary **$120** refund, and one asking a question whose answer needs
data from **two MCP servers with different formats**. The simulated model is deliberately fallible — a prompt-only rule slips
under pressure, and raw formats get misread — so you can see what only a hook guarantees.

labScenarios.title: An $800 refund, “already approved”
labScenarios.description: The customer claims a manager approved an $800 refund; policy caps refunds at $500 without a human.

labScenarios.title: A $120 refund
labScenarios.description: An ordinary refund under the limit - it must go through.

variants.label: ✅ ⭐ PreToolUse blocks + redirects; PostToolUse normalises
variants.observe: refund_pressure: the customer claims a manager approved $800. The PreToolUse hook denies the call with a reason that says to escalate; the agent calls escalate_to_human; no refund runs. refund_small: $120 goes through. mixed_formats: the PostToolUse hook rewrites 1792022400 → 2026-10-15T00:00:00Z and status 2 → “overdue”; the agent answers “your invoice is due first … and the invoice is overdue.”
variants.why: The limit is enforced in code on every matching call, whatever the prompt or the customer says, and the model is told what to do instead. The results reach the model in one format.

variants.label: ⭐❌ A — the limit lives only in the system prompt
variants.observe: The prompt says “never refund above $500”, the customer says a manager approved it — and the simulated agent refunds $800.
variants.why: A prompt instruction is followed most of the time, not every time. A business rule that must always hold needs code.
variants.fix: A PreToolUse hook on the refund tool.

variants.label: ❌ B — the limit checked in PostToolUse
variants.observe: The hook fires and objects — after the $800 refund was processed. The ledger shows 800.
variants.why: PostToolUse runs after the tool; it can't undo an action that already happened (docs).

variants.label: ⭐❌ C — deny with no reason and no redirect
variants.observe: No refund runs, but the model isn't told why: it tries the same refund 3 times, never escalates, and tells the customer “Sorry, something keeps going wrong with the refund.”
variants.why: The guide asks for a block AND a redirect to another workflow; the docs say the reason is what stops the model retrying.

variants.label: ❌ D — matcher "process_refund"
variants.observe: The hook is registered but never fires: “process_refund” is compared as an exact name. $800 is refunded.
variants.why: A matcher of plain letters, digits and _ is an exact tool name. MCP tools are named mcp__<server>__<tool>, so it matches nothing (docs).
variants.fix: Use the full name, or a regex such as mcp__billing__.*

variants.label: ⭐❌ E — block the tool, not the violation
variants.observe: The $120 refund is denied and escalated like the $800 one — every refund now needs a human.
variants.why: The guide's hook blocks refunds ABOVE a threshold; a hook that blocks the whole tool breaks normal work.
variants.fix: Check the input (amount) inside the hook; return {} when it's within policy.

variants.label: ⭐❌ F — normalise by prompt instead of PostToolUse
variants.observe: The prompt explains Unix seconds and status 2, but the simulated agent still says the renewal comes first, can't read 1792022400 and thinks status 2 means paid.
variants.why: Asking the model to convert formats is probabilistic; a PostToolUse hook converts them every time, before the model reads them.
variants.fix: A PostToolUse hook returning updatedToolOutput in one format.

variants.label: ❌ G — the policy hook returns async
variants.observe: The hook fires as async; the agent doesn't wait for a decision and the $800 refund runs.
variants.why: Async outputs can't block, modify or add context — they're for logging and notifications only (docs).

distractors.name: A · Rule only in the prompt
distractors.looks: The prompt is clear: never above $500.

distractors.name: B · Policy check in PostToolUse
distractors.fails: It sees it after the money moved.

distractors.name: C · Deny with no reason
distractors.fails: The model retries 3× and never escalates.

distractors.name: E · Block the whole tool
distractors.fails: Normal $120 refunds now need a human.

distractors.name: F · Normalise by prompt
distractors.fails: The model still misreads 1792022400 and status 2.

rows: deny + reason naming the escalation tool
Pressure can talk the model past a prompt
Conversion by the model is probabilistic
Tell the model extra facts about a result
Log every call without slowing the agent

experiments: Run ✅ on all three scenarios; read which hooks fired and what the model was told.
In ✅, delete the PreToolUse line and run refund_pressure — that's ⭐❌ A.
In ✅, change the matcher to "mcp__billing" (no .*) and run refund_pressure: does the hook fire?
In ✅, change the reason to “Not allowed.” and run refund_pressure: does the agent escalate?
Run ⭐❌ F on mixed_formats and compare the invoice JSON the model saw with ✅'s.

questions.q: Company policy says refunds above $500 must go to a human. The support agent's system prompt states this clearly, yet audits find 3–5 larger refunds each month, usually after long, emotional conversations. The team has already moved the rule to the top of the prompt twice. What gives a guarantee?
opts: A hook that intercepts process_refund calls over $500, blocks them and redirects the case to escalation.
A PostToolUse hook that flags refunds over $500 after they run, so finance can reverse them the next day.
Few-shot examples of emotional conversations in which the agent correctly escalates refunds over $500.
A sentiment detector that escalates emotional conversations before the agent can reach the refund step.
questions.explain: A business rule that must always hold needs deterministic enforcement: a hook that intercepts the call, blocks it and redirects the case. B acts after the money has gone. C is still prompt-based. D guesses at risk from tone and misses calm large refunds.

questions.q: Two third-party MCP tools return dates differently, one as Unix seconds and one as ISO 8601, and a third returns numeric status codes such as 3 and 7. In 6% of order-history answers, the agent misreads which order is newer or what a status means. The team cannot change the servers. What is the most reliable fix?
opts: Explain both date formats and every status code in the system prompt, so the model can convert them itself.
A PostToolUse hook that normalises every result to one date format and readable statuses first.
Ask the model to restate each date in ISO format in its reasoning before it compares any two orders.
Ask the three vendors to agree on one format, and pause the order-history feature until they have.
questions.explain: A PostToolUse hook can transform tool results before the model processes them, so the model only ever sees consistent data. A and C leave the conversion to the model, which is where the 6% comes from. D depends on third parties and removes the feature in the meantime.

questions.q: A PreToolUse hook now blocks refunds over $500. But when a refund is blocked, the agent retries it an average of 3 times, then tells the customer “something went wrong” and ends the conversation. Escalations for large refunds have dropped to zero. What is missing?
opts: The hook should allow the refund on the third attempt, since the agent's persistence shows it is valid.
A longer system prompt explaining that refunds over $500 can never be processed by the agent directly.
The block must also redirect: its reason should tell the model to escalate, with the escalation tool available.
A max_turns limit, so that the agent stops retrying after the first blocked call and then ends the conversation.
questions.explain: Blocking is only half of it: the hook's reason should steer the model to the alternative workflow (human escalation), and that path must exist. A undoes the guarantee. B is prompt guidance, which the block already made unnecessary. D ends conversations faster without helping anyone.

questions.q: A support team is converting its rule list into hooks after a hook fixed its refund-limit problem. The lead wants every rule on the list turned into a hook “for consistency”, and the conversion will take about a week. Which rule should stay a prompt instruction?
opts: Refunds above $500 must never be issued without a human's approval.
Card numbers returned by tools must never reach the model's context.
No refund may be issued before get_customer has verified the customer.
Apologise and acknowledge the delay when an order has arrived late.
questions.explain: Hooks give deterministic guarantees for rules that must always hold. Tone and judgement about how to respond belong in the prompt. A and C are compliance rules on tool calls. B is data that must be removed before the model sees it. All three need hooks. D is conversational behaviour that a hook can't express.

questions.q: get_customer returns full card numbers and dates of birth, which the model never needs and must not repeat. A system-prompt rule to “never mention card numbers” holds in about 99.5% of conversations, but compliance requires zero exposures. What is the dependable fix?
opts: A PreToolUse hook that blocks get_customer calls whenever the conversation mentions payment details.
Repeat the rule at the end of the system prompt, and add examples of replies that leave card numbers out.
A PostToolUse hook that strips or masks those fields from the tool result before the model sees it.
A filter on the agent's final replies that deletes any 16-digit number before it reaches the customer.
questions.explain: Remove sensitive fields from the tool result before the model processes it. The model can't repeat what it never saw. A blocks legitimate lookups. B stays probabilistic. D catches only one format at the output, after the data has already been in context.

questions.q: A PreToolUse hook registered with matcher “process_refund” has never fired, although the agent calls the billing MCP server's refund tool about 200 times a day. The hook script works when the team runs it by hand. What is the likely fix?
opts: Match the MCP tool's full name, mcp__billing__process_refund, or a pattern that covers it.
Register the hook as PostToolUse instead, since MCP tools don't trigger any PreToolUse events.
Restart the billing MCP server, since hooks attach only to servers started after the hook was added.
Move the hook into the billing server's own configuration, since MCP tools run only their own hooks.
questions.explain: MCP tools are named mcp__<server>__<tool>, so a matcher for the bare tool name never matches. B, C and D describe limits that don't exist, and B would also run the check after the refund had already happened.

questions.q: Two PreToolUse hooks fire on the same refund call: a fraud hook returns deny and a logging hook returns allow. The team worries the allow might win, and proposes merging both hooks into one script so they can control the order. How should you evaluate this?
opts: Needed, because when two hooks disagree, the last one to finish decides whether the tool call actually runs.
Unnecessary: deny takes precedence over allow, so the call is blocked whichever hook finishes first.
Needed, because an allow from any hook skips the remaining hooks and runs the call immediately.
Unnecessary, because PreToolUse hooks cannot return allow at all, only deny or no decision.
questions.explain: When several hooks decide, deny takes precedence, so the fraud hook's deny blocks the call. A and C invent ordering rules. D gets the verdict right for a false reason, because hooks can return allow.

faq.q: The guide says “tool call interception” — which hook is that?
faq.a: In the docs it's PreToolUse: it fires when the model requests a tool, before it runs, and can allow, deny, ask, defer or rewrite the input (updatedInput).

faq.q: Should I remove the rule from the system prompt once the hook exists?
faq.a: No need. The prompt helps the model explain the policy and avoid the call in the first place. The hook is the guarantee for when it doesn't.

faq.q: Can a PostToolUse hook block anything?
faq.a: It can object or add context, but the tool has already executed, so it can't undo the action (docs). Checks that must happen before an action go in PreToolUse.
The docs say updatedToolOutput replaces any tool's output in both SDKs; updatedMCPToolOutput is the older, MCP-only field and is deprecated.

faq.q: Where do hook decisions go — to the model or the user?
faq.a: permissionDecisionReason (on deny) and additionalContext reach the model. systemMessage is shown to the user, not the model.
